genes/0.notes: CERT1 was called COL4A3BP until HGNC renamed it in 2019, so the founding literature indexes the gene under the old symbol; both must be searched. The disease alleles are heterozygous missense changes clustered in the autoregulatory apparatus and act by gain of function, so this entry must not be read as a haploinsufficiency disorder. The corollary matters for variant interpretation: a rare or even truncating CERT1 variant is not evidence of MRD34 on its own. The C-terminal frameshift c.2242_2243dupAA p.(Pro749fs) segregated away from intellectual disability in its family and left CERT phosphorylation, activity and localisation intact in knock-in cells, and the authors used it as a disease-matched negative control. The disease alleles are not scattered across the protein. Twenty-seven of the 31 enrolled patients carried a variant in the region between the pleckstrin homology and the C-terminal START-related domain, and those variants populate four spatial clusters: the first serines of the serine-rich region (p.S132, p.S135, p.S138, p.S141), p.T166, residues 240 to 254 including the recurrent p.G243, and the C-terminal end of the FFAT motif (p.V326F, p.A329P, p.L330V, p.L330P). Broad genotype-phenotype correlation follows that structure, with p.S132 and p.S135 at the severe end and p.S138, p.T166 and p.G243 associated with normal early milestones followed by regression or slowing. Per-allele case counts for individual variants are in the cohort paper's supplemental tables and are not reproduced here.

evidence.snippet: The utility of the method was demonstrated by a library of 140 derivatives of the CERT inhibitor HPA-12. treatments/6.description: Preclinical only. evidence.snippet: inhibiting CERT pharmacologically corrects morphological and motor abnormalities in a Drosophila model of the disease, which we call ceramide transporter (CerTra) syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Pharmacological inhibition of the activated transporter reverses the model phenotype, which is the target-validation evidence for this link.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: The proposed therapeutic node: an inhibitor reduces the excess transfer activity that the disease variants create.

open_questions/0.rationale: The chain from constitutively active CERT to increased sphingomyelin synthesis is demonstrated in cells, and the clinical phenotype is established, but nothing connects them at cellular resolution in human tissue. Neurons, neural progenitors, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes and Schwann cells are all plausible on expression grounds. No patient-derived iPSC neuron, cerebral organoid, single-cell atlas or human neural lipidomic study of this disorder exists, so the entry deliberately binds only neuron at this node rather than asserting a primary cell type.

open_questions/1.rationale: The only in vivo evidence that CERT inhibition is therapeutic comes from a fly. Drosophila has no cortical expansion, no myelinating oligodendrocytes and no language, so the readouts corrected in the model are not the manifestations that matter clinically. There is also a timing problem the model cannot address: the human phenotype is developmental, so a drug given after diagnosis acts on a nervous system already built under excess CERT activity. Finally, CERT is required for normal membrane lipid homeostasis in every tissue, so the therapeutic window in a developing human is unknown and over-inhibition is a plausible harm rather than a theoretical one.

open_questions/2.rationale: Every published individual was ascertained through rare-disease referral or matchmaking, so there is no denominator. Because the phenotype is nonspecific and the causal alleles are missense rather than truncating, the disorder is exactly the kind that accumulates undiagnosed among people labelled with nonsyndromic developmental delay. A denominator would require systematic CERT1 review in an unselected sequenced intellectual-disability cohort, with mechanism-aware variant interpretation rather than a loss-of-function filter.

open_questions/3.rationale: The single neuropathological study of this disorder found choroid plexus epithelial disorganisation with reduced aquaporin-1, cysts and calcification, plus perivascular spaces distended with proteinaceous material, and raised the possibility of disturbed CSF dynamics and impaired perivascular clearance. That is a mechanistically attractive extension of a membrane-lipid disorder, but it rests on one case that was also complicated by sudden unexplained death in childhood, and the authors themselves state it only as a possibility. It should not be curated as a phenotype of the disorder until replicated.

steps/11.description: CEP85L localizes to the pericentriolar material of the maternal centriole and is required cell-autonomously for cortical neuronal migration; knockdown of the mouse orthologue produces a neuronal migration defect. The malformation heterozygous CEP85L variants cause is posterior-predominant, matching the topography of PAFAH1B1 disease, which places the lesion at the centrosome rather than on the dynein regulator itself.

evidence.snippet: Functional analysis of the p.V162SfsX19 mutation, using a yeast complementation assay, showed loss-of-function of the mutant CDK5 gene product, thereby implicating its role in the pathogenesis of autosomal recessive LCH in the studied family.
evidence.explanation: Supports the loss of CDK5 kinase function bound on this node and ties it to the human recessive lissencephaly phenotype.

evidence.snippet: it forms a complex with many other proteins required for migration, including CDK5, LIS1, NDE1, KIF2A, and DYNC1H1
evidence.explanation: Places CDK5 in a physical complex with LIS1 and the dynein heavy chain, which is the basis for the downstream edge to the nucleokinesis node.

steps/12.description: CDK5 is a cyclin-dependent kinase that forms a complex with LIS1, NDE1, KIF2A and the dynein heavy chain, all of which are required for neuronal migration. Its activity is reduced either by biallelic loss-of-function CDK5 alleles or by loss of CEP85L, which is needed for CDK5 to be correctly localized and activated at the centrosome. Human biallelic CDK5 null alleles cause lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia, so the kinase is required for cortical migration in humans and not only in model systems.

evidence.snippet: recombinant αN-catenin interacted with purified actin and repressed ARP2/3 actin-branching activity
evidence.explanation: Establishes that αN-catenin represses ARP2/3 actin branching, so its loss increases the two actin processes bound on this node.

evidence.snippet: The actin-binding domain of αN-catenin or ARP2/3 inhibitors rescued the neuronal phenotype associated with CTNNA2 loss, suggesting ARP2/3 de-repression as a potential disease mechanism.
evidence.explanation: The rescue by ARP2/3 inhibition is what makes de-repression the mechanism this node asserts rather than a correlated observation.

steps/13.description: CTNNA2 encodes αN-catenin, which binds actin and represses ARP2/3-driven actin branching. Biallelic truncating CTNNA2 alleles remove that repression, and the neuronal phenotype is rescued either by the actin-binding domain of αN-catenin or by ARP2/3 inhibitors. This is an actin-side mechanism and is distinct from the microtubule and dynein lesions that the tubulin, PAFAH1B1 and DCX subtypes share.

evidence.snippet: Since microtubule (MT) and actin-associated proteins play important functions in regulating the dynamics of MT and actin cytoskeletons during neuronal migration, genetic mutations or deletions of crucial genes involved in cytoskeletal processes lead to lissencephaly in human and neuronal migration defects in mouse.
evidence.explanation: Supports cytoskeletal/microtubule dysfunction as the molecular basis for the migration defect underlying lissencephaly.

evidence.snippet: During neuronal migration, MT organization and transport are controlled by platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase isoform 1b regulatory subunit 1 (PAFAH1B1, formerly known as LIS1, Lissencephaly-1), doublecortin (DCX), YWHAE, and tubulin.
evidence.explanation: Names the key microtubule-regulating proteins (LIS1/PAFAH1B1, DCX, tubulin) whose mutations cause classic lissencephaly.

evidence.snippet: Thus, we report variants of the microtubule-binding GAR domain of MACF1 as the cause of a distinctive and most likely pathognomonic brain malformation.

evidence.explanation: Supports binding DYNC1H1 to this node by placing the dynein heavy chain in the same migration-required complex as LIS1, which this node already models.

steps/14.description: Neuronal migration depends on microtubule and actin cytoskeletal dynamics and on the dynein motor and its regulators. Mutations in microtubule subunits (tubulins) and in microtubule/dynein-associated proteins such as PAFAH1B1 (LIS1) and DCX impair microtubule organization, transport and nucleokinesis, the coupling of the nucleus to the centrosome that drives forward movement of migrating neurons.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate that LIS1 directly interacts with the cytoplasmic dynein heavy chain (CDHC) and NUDEL
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the core LIS1-NUDEL-dynein molecular complex underlying the neuronal migration branch.

evidence.snippet: recombinant Lis1 binds to native brain dynein and significantly increases the microtubule-stimulated enzymatic activity of dynein in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Shows that LIS1 directly modulates dynein enzymatic activity, connecting PAFAH1B1 loss to microtubule motor dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: Mice with one inactive allele display cortical, hippocampal and olfactory bulb disorganization resulting from delayed neuronal migration by a cell-autonomous neuronal pathway.
evidence.explanation: Supports dosage-sensitive LIS1 neuronal migration failure in vivo.

steps/15.description: PAFAH1B1/LIS1 dosage loss disrupts a LIS1-NUDEL-cytoplasmic dynein heavy chain complex that normally regulates dynein on microtubules during neuronal migration. The resulting defect impairs centrosome-nucleus coupling and nucleokinesis in migrating cortical neurons, producing the classical type I lissencephaly/SBH migration-arrest branch. Mouse allelic series show that lower Pafah1b1 activity causes progressively more severe neuronal migration and brain-organization defects, matching the clinical severity gradient from pachygyria/SBH toward more severe lissencephaly.

evidence.snippet: X-linked lissencephaly and "double cortex" are allelic human disorders mapping to Xq22.3-Xq23 associated with arrest of migrating cerebral cortical neurons.
evidence.explanation: Establishes DCX-related lissencephaly and double-cortex/SBH as allelic human neuronal-migration arrest disorders.

evidence.snippet: DCX coassembles with brain microtubules, and recombinant DCX stimulates the polymerization of purified tubulin.
evidence.explanation: Supports the microtubule-stabilization and tubulin-polymerization branch of DCX disease biology.

evidence.snippet: DCX likely directs neuronal migration by regulating the organization and stability of microtubules.
evidence.explanation: Links DCX microtubule organization and stability to neuronal migration.

steps/16.description: DCX encodes a neuronal microtubule-associated protein required for normal migration of cortical neurons. Pathogenic DCX variants impair the microtubule-stabilizing and tubulin-polymerizing function of doublecortin, slowing or arresting migration. Hemizygous males usually develop anterior-predominant classic lissencephaly, whereas heterozygous females often develop subcortical band heterotopia through X-linked mosaicism.

evidence.snippet: Lis1 is essential for precise control of mitotic spindle orientation in both neuroepithelial stem cells and radial glial progenitor cells.
evidence.explanation: Supports a LIS1 progenitor-spindle branch in neuroepithelial and radial glial progenitors.

evidence.snippet: control of symmetric division, essential for neuroepithelial stem cell proliferation, is mediated through spindle orientation determined via LIS1/NDEL1/dynein-mediated cortical microtubule capture.
evidence.explanation: Links the progenitor division phenotype to the LIS1/NDEL1/dynein microtubule-capture mechanism.

steps/17.description: In addition to the postmitotic neuronal migration branch, PAFAH1B1/LIS1 loss perturbs neuroepithelial and radial-glial progenitor mitotic spindle orientation through LIS1/NDEL1/dynein-mediated cortical microtubule capture. This progenitor branch affects symmetric division, progenitor expansion and cortical neuron output, explaining why PAFAH1B1 disease can include cortical thickness, simplified gyration and severity features not captured by a migration-only model.

evidence.snippet: An autosomal recessive form of lissencephaly (LCH) associated with severe abnormalities of the cerebellum, hippocampus and brainstem maps to chromosome 7q22, and is associated with two independent mutations in the human gene encoding reelin (RELN).
evidence.explanation: Establishes RELN loss of function as a recessive cause of lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: RELN encodes a large (388 kD) secreted protein that acts on migrating cortical neurons by binding to the very low density lipoprotein receptor (VLDLR), the apolipoprotein E receptor 2 (ApoER2; refs 9-11 ), alpha3beta1 integrin and protocadherins.
evidence.explanation: Describes the molecular mechanism by which reelin signaling guides migrating cortical neurons, lost in RELN-related lissencephaly.

steps/18.description: RELN encodes the large secreted glycoprotein reelin, which acts on migrating cortical neurons by binding lipoprotein receptors (VLDLR and ApoER2). Loss-of-function RELN mutations cause an autosomal recessive lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia, reflecting reelin's role in directing cortical neuronal migration and laminar positioning.

evidence.snippet: Mitotic spindle formation is defective in patient-derived fibroblasts, a consequence of disrupted interactions of mutant KATNB1 with KATNA1, the catalytic subunit of Katanin, and other microtubule-associated proteins.
evidence.explanation: Supports the abnormal mitotic spindle organization bound on this node, measured in cells from affected individuals, and names katanin as the severing enzyme whose regulation is lost.

evidence.snippet: kat80 loss specifically affects the asymmetrically dividing neuroblasts, which display supernumerary centrosomes and spindle abnormalities during mitosis
evidence.explanation: Supports locating the defect in the dividing progenitor compartment that this node binds, shown in the Drosophila ortholog.

steps/19.description: KATNB1 encodes the regulatory p80 subunit of the microtubule-severing enzyme katanin. Biallelic deleterious KATNB1 alleles disrupt its interaction with the catalytic subunit KATNA1 and with other microtubule-associated proteins, and patient-derived fibroblasts show defective mitotic spindle formation. The lesion is therefore in the dividing progenitor rather than in the locomotion of an already postmitotic neuron, which is consistent with microcephaly being what loss of the orthologs reproduces in zebrafish and flies.

evidence.snippet: Lissencephaly ("smooth brain," from "lissos," meaning smooth, and "encephalos," meaning brain) is a severe developmental disorder in which neuronal migration is impaired, leading to a thickened cerebral cortex whose normally folded contour is simplified and smooth.
evidence.explanation: Establishes impaired neuronal migration as the core mechanism producing the thickened, smooth cortex that defines the lissencephaly spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Failure or delay in neuronal migration causes severe abnormalities in cortical layering, which consequently results in human lissencephaly ('smooth brain'), a neuronal migration disorder.
evidence.explanation: Directly links failure/delay of neuronal migration to the abnormal cortical lamination that characterizes lissencephaly.

steps/20.description: Pathogenic variants in genes governing cytoskeletal dynamics and neuronal migration disrupt the long-range radial migration of postmitotic cortical neurons from the proliferative ventricular zone to their final laminar position. The resulting failure or delay of migration produces a thickened, smooth (agyric/pachygyric) cortex with disordered six-layered lamination.

evidence.snippet: Cortical dysplasia results from neuroglial overmigration into the arachnoid space, forming an extracortical layer, responsible for agyria and/or 'cobblestone' brain surface and ventricular enlargement. The underlying mechanism is a disruption of the glia limitans, the outermost layer of the brain.
evidence.explanation: A fetal neuropathological series states the overmigration direction and the boundary lesion that this node asserts, distinguishing it from migration arrest.

evidence.snippet: The most severe, which we called cobblestone lissencephaly A, was linked to mutations in POMT1 (34%), POMT2 (8%) and FKRP (1.5%). The least severe, cobblestone lissencephaly C, was linked to POMGNT1 mutations (18%).
evidence.explanation: Attaches POMT1, POMT2 and POMGNT1 to the human cobblestone phenotype in a genotyped fetal cohort, which is what justifies binding those three genes to this node.

evidence.snippet: Our data suggest that loss of TMTC3 causes COB with minimal eye or muscle involvement.
evidence.explanation: Attaches TMTC3 to the same cobblestone endpoint while separating it clinically from the dystroglycanopathies, which is why both routes are bound to one node here.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in POMT1, POMT2, POMGNT1, LARGE, FKTN and FKRP genes attributed these diseases to alpha-dystroglycanopathies.
evidence.explanation: Supports the claim in this node's description that POMT1, POMT2 and POMGNT1 reach the cobblestone endpoint through alpha-dystroglycan, where TMTC3 does not. Recorded as BACKGROUND because it is the cited study's summary of prior gene discoveries rather than its own result.

steps/21.description: In the cobblestone forms the cortical pial boundary fails rather than locomotion, and neurons and glia migrate past the cortical surface into the arachnoid space, forming an extracortical layer. This is the opposite direction of error from the migration-arrest nodes above and is why cobblestone malformation is kept separate from classic lissencephaly in this entry. TMTC3 reaches this node without an alpha-dystroglycan defect, while the glycosylation-pathway genes on the Cobblestone subtype reach it through alpha-dystroglycan.

evidence.snippet: Cobblestone lissencephaly (COB) is a severe brain malformation in which overmigration of neurons and glial cells into the arachnoid space results in the formation of cortical dysplasia.
evidence.explanation: Defines the phenotype bound here. Recorded as BACKGROUND because the sentence is the cited report's framing of an established definition rather than its own finding, which is the TMTC3 gene discovery.

steps/22.description: Cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly, in which neurons and glia overmigrate past the pial boundary into the arachnoid space and form an extracortical layer with a nodular brain surface. Present in the TMTC3 and glycosylation-pathway subtypes and absent from the migration-arrest forms.

edges/12.description: Disruption of the LIS1/DCX/tubulin microtubule machinery impairs the nucleokinesis and somal translocation that radially migrating cortical neurons require, producing the migration arrest underlying lissencephaly.

edges/13.description: Disruption of the LIS1-NUDEL-dynein motor pathway impairs nucleokinesis and radial migration, converging on the lissencephaly cortical-lamination defect.

edges/14.description: Loss of DCX microtubule stabilization disrupts migration of cortical neurons, producing lissencephaly or subcortical band heterotopia depending on sex, mosaicism, and variant context.

edges/15.description: The progenitor-spindle branch changes cortical neuron output and cortical organization, worsening the same abnormal cortical lamination endpoint as the neuronal migration branch.

edges/16.description: Loss of reelin signaling to migrating cortical neurons disrupts the orderly inside-out cortical lamination, producing the migration defect underlying RELN-related lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: Loss of CEP85L disrupts CDK5 localization and activation, leading to centrosome disorganization and disrupted microtubule cytoskeleton organization.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from CEP85L loss to failed CDK5 activation that this edge asserts.

edges/17.description: Loss of CEP85L disrupts the localization and activation of CDK5 at the centrosome, so the pericentriolar defect is transmitted to the kinase that the nucleokinesis module depends on.

evidence.snippet: Loss of CEP85L disrupts CDK5 localization and activation, leading to centrosome disorganization and disrupted microtubule cytoskeleton organization.
evidence.explanation: Supports the step from failed CDK5 activation to disorganized centrosome and microtubule cytoskeleton, which is what the nucleokinesis node models.

edges/18.description: Reduced CDK5 activity disorganizes the centrosome and the microtubule cytoskeleton, so nucleokinesis fails by the same route as in PAFAH1B1 disease even though the scaffold protein itself is intact.

evidence.snippet: Exome sequencing analysis of over 2,000 children with complex malformations of cortical development identified five independent (four homozygous and one compound heterozygous) deleterious mutations in KATNB1, encoding the regulatory subunit of the microtubule-severing enzyme Katanin.
evidence.explanation: Links biallelic KATNB1 loss to complex malformations of cortical development in humans, which is the consequence this edge asserts.

edges/19.description: Spindle and centrosome abnormalities in dividing neural progenitors reduce and mis-time the output of migrating neurons, producing the cortical malformation seen in KATNB1 disease.

evidence.snippet: CTNNA2 was expressed in human cerebral cortex, and its loss in neurons led to defects in neurite stability and migration.
evidence.explanation: States the migration defect that follows CTNNA2 loss, which is the consequence this edge asserts.

edges/20.description: Unrestrained ARP2/3 activity destabilizes neurites and impairs cortical neuronal migration, producing the recessive pachygyria of the CTNNA2 subtype.

evidence.snippet: Cortical dysplasia results from neuroglial overmigration into the arachnoid space, forming an extracortical layer, responsible for agyria and/or 'cobblestone' brain surface and ventricular enlargement. The underlying mechanism is a disruption of the glia limitans, the outermost layer of the brain.
evidence.explanation: States the step from overmigration to the cobblestone brain surface that this edge asserts.

edges/21.description: Neuroglial overmigration past the pial boundary produces the extracortical layer and nodular brain surface that define cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly.

evidence.snippet: LIS1 accounted for 40% of patients, followed by DCX (23%), TUBA1A (5%), and DYNC1H1 (3%).
evidence.explanation: LIS1/PAFAH1B1 is the most common genetic cause of lissencephaly in an 811-patient cohort.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of PAFAH1B1-related lissencephaly/SBH is established in a proband with a heterozygous pathogenic variant in PAFAH1B1 identified by molecular genetic testing.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms heterozygous PAFAH1B1 pathogenic variants as causal for classic lissencephaly/SBH.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of a DCX-related disorder is established in a proband with a DCX pathogenic variant identified by molecular genetic testing.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms DCX pathogenic variants as causal for X-linked lissencephaly/SBH.

evidence.snippet: LIS1 accounted for 40% of patients, followed by DCX (23%), TUBA1A (5%), and DYNC1H1 (3%).
evidence.explanation: DCX is the second most common lissencephaly gene in a large cohort.

evidence.snippet: LIS1 accounted for 40% of patients, followed by DCX (23%), TUBA1A (5%), and DYNC1H1 (3%).
evidence.explanation: TUBA1A is an established lissencephaly gene and the most common tubulin-gene cause in this cohort.

evidence.snippet: LIS1 accounted for 40% of patients, followed by DCX (23%), TUBA1A (5%), and DYNC1H1 (3%).
evidence.explanation: DYNC1H1, encoding the dynein heavy chain, is a recognized lissencephaly gene consistent with the dynein/migration mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The mutations disrupt splicing of RELN cDNA, resulting in low or undetectable amounts of reelin protein.
evidence.explanation: Documents RELN loss-of-function (splicing-disrupting) variants causing recessive lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: Many were tested for deletion 17p13.3 and mutations of LIS1, DCX, and ARX, but few other genes.
evidence.explanation: ARX is an established X-linked lissencephaly gene included in standard diagnostic testing.

evidence.snippet: We now implicate CEP85L as an important cause of posterior predominant LIS, identifying 13 individuals with rare, heterozygous CEP85L variants, including 2 families with autosomal dominant inheritance.
evidence.explanation: Establishes heterozygous CEP85L variants as causal for posterior-predominant lissencephaly in 13 individuals.

evidence.snippet: CEP85L | HGNC:21638 | lissencephaly 10 | MONDO:0030031 | AD | Definitive | SOP11 | Brain Malformations Gene Curation Expert Panel
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the CEP85L gene-disease relationship as Definitive.

genes/6.notes: CEP85L is a pericentriolar-material protein. Its loss disrupts the localization and activation of CDK5 at the centrosome, which places it upstream of the same LIS1-NDEL1-dynein nucleokinesis machinery that the classic subtype depends on.

evidence.snippet: we identified a homozygous splice site mutation g.IVS8+1G>A in cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5), causing complete skipping of exon 8, and leading to a frame shift and premature stop codon (p.V162SfsX19).
evidence.explanation: Records the specific homozygous null allele that establishes CDK5 as a recessive lissencephaly gene.

evidence.snippet: Functional analysis of the p.V162SfsX19 mutation, using a yeast complementation assay, showed loss-of-function of the mutant CDK5 gene product, thereby implicating its role in the pathogenesis of autosomal recessive LCH in the studied family.
evidence.explanation: Supports the loss-of-function association recorded on this record rather than a gain or altered function.

genes/7.notes: CDK5 is a member of the migration complex that also contains LIS1, NDE1, KIF2A and the dynein heavy chain, so a biallelic null allele removes a kinase the classic PAFAH1B1 machinery depends on rather than the scaffold itself.

evidence.snippet: Exome sequencing analysis of over 2,000 children with complex malformations of cortical development identified five independent (four homozygous and one compound heterozygous) deleterious mutations in KATNB1, encoding the regulatory subunit of the microtubule-severing enzyme Katanin.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic deleterious KATNB1 alleles as a cause of complex cortical malformation.

evidence.snippet: Mitotic spindle formation is defective in patient-derived fibroblasts, a consequence of disrupted interactions of mutant KATNB1 with KATNA1, the catalytic subunit of Katanin, and other microtubule-associated proteins.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived fibroblasts localize the defect to mitotic spindle formation, supporting the loss-of-function association recorded here.

genes/8.notes: KATNB1 is the regulatory subunit of katanin. Patient fibroblasts show defective mitotic spindle formation, which places this gene with the progenitor-division mechanism rather than with locomotion of an already postmitotic neuron.

evidence.snippet: We discovered heterozygous de novo missense variants or an in-frame deletion involving highly conserved zinc-binding residues within the GAR domain of MACF1 in the first eight subjects.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the variant class and domain, supporting the dominant de novo mechanism recorded here.

evidence.snippet: MACF1 | HGNC:13664 | lissencephaly spectrum disorder with complex brainstem malformation | MONDO:0100472 | AD | Moderate | SOP9 | Brain Malformations Gene Curation Expert Panel
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies MACF1 as Moderate for this malformation under autosomal dominant inheritance.

genes/9.notes: The reported variants are heterozygous, de novo, and concentrated in conserved zinc-binding residues of the microtubule-binding GAR domain. The founding report proposes a gain-of-function or dominant-negative mechanism rather than haploinsufficiency, on the grounds that truncating MACF1 alleles are present in population sequencing data, so this record is left as "Pathogenic variant" rather than asserting loss of function.

evidence.snippet: Our screening of a cohort of 25 families with recessive forms of COB identified six families affected by biallelic mutations in TMTC3 (encoding transmembrane and tetratricopeptide repeat containing 3), a gene without obvious functional connections to alpha-dystroglycan.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic TMTC3 variants in six families as a recessive cause of cobblestone lissencephaly.

genes/10.notes: TMTC3 loss produces a cobblestone malformation, so this gene acts on the overmigration route rather than the migration-arrest route that PAFAH1B1, DCX and the tubulins share. The founding report states it has no obvious functional connection to alpha-dystroglycan, which separates it from the glycosylation-pathway genes on the Cobblestone subtype.

evidence.snippet: Here, we identify biallelic truncating mutations in CTNNA2, encoding αN-catenin, in patients with a distinct recessive form of pachygyria.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic truncating CTNNA2 variants as causal for a recessive pachygyria, supporting the loss-of-function association recorded here.

genes/11.notes: CTNNA2 encodes αN-catenin. The reported alleles are biallelic and truncating, and the mechanism proposed is de-repression of ARP2/3-driven actin branching rather than a microtubule defect.

evidence.snippet: polytherapy with valproic acid and lamotrigine appears most effective in reducing drug-resistant seizures
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends valproic acid plus lamotrigine polytherapy for drug-resistant seizures in PAFAH1B1-related lissencephaly.

treatments/0.description: Standard anti-seizure medication selected by seizure type; in PAFAH1B1-related lissencephaly, polytherapy with valproic acid and lamotrigine appears most effective for drug-resistant seizures. Seizures are often refractory.

evidence.snippet: placement of a gastrostomy tube for those with failure to thrive, dysphagia, and/or recurrent aspiration pneumonia
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends gastrostomy for feeding failure and aspiration risk in lissencephaly.

treatments/1.description: Placement of a gastrostomy tube for individuals with failure to thrive, dysphagia, and/or recurrent aspiration pneumonia, with feeding strategies for newborns with poor suck and swallow.

evidence.snippet: physical therapy to promote mobility and prevent contractures
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends physical therapy to support mobility and prevent contractures in DCX-related disorders.

treatments/2.description: Physical therapy to promote mobility and prevent contractures; in patient cohorts physiotherapy is reported among the most effective supportive therapies.

evidence.snippet: occupational therapy to improve fine motor skills
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends occupational therapy to improve fine and oral motor skills in DCX-related lissencephaly.

treatments/3.description: Occupational therapy to improve fine motor skills and oral motor control, as part of multidisciplinary supportive management of lissencephaly.

evidence.snippet: participation in speech therapy
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews includes speech therapy in the supportive management of DCX-related lissencephaly.

treatments/4.description: Speech therapy to support communication and oral-motor function as part of multidisciplinary supportive management.

evidence.snippet: Once the DCX pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports genetic counseling with prenatal/preimplantation testing once the familial variant is known.

treatments/5.description: Genetic counseling and reproductive options (prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing) once a familial pathogenic variant is identified; important given the high de novo rate and variable inheritance across the spectrum.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that LIS1 and NUDEL regulate CDHC activity during neuronal migration and axonal retrograde transport in a Cdk5/p35-dependent fashion.
evidence.explanation: Supports the LIS1/NUDEL/dynein branch as a distinct molecular mechanism within the shared migration-failure endpoint.

evidence.snippet: Lis1 is essential for precise control of mitotic spindle orientation in both neuroepithelial stem cells and radial glial progenitor cells.
evidence.explanation: Supports a PAFAH1B1/LIS1 progenitor branch not captured by a purely postmitotic migration model.

evidence.snippet: classic thick lissencephaly (more severe anteriorly), usually in males, and subcortical band heterotopia (SBH), primarily in females.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the DCX anterior-predominant and sex-biased SBH pattern.

open_questions/0.rationale: PAFAH1B1/LIS1 and DCX share a migration-failure endpoint, but the human radiographic gradients and cellular branches differ: PAFAH1B1 has a LIS1/NUDEL/dynein motor branch plus a progenitor-spindle component, whereas DCX disease is typically anterior-predominant in males and SBH in heterozygous females. The unresolved issue is whether regional expression, different microtubule-motor versus lattice functions, X-inactivation mosaicism, or human-specific progenitor context best explains these genotype-specific patterns.

evidence.snippet: Dcx mutant mice show neocortical lamination that is largely indistinguishable from wild type and show normal patterns of neocortical neurogenesis and neuronal migration.
evidence.explanation: The founding germline Dcx-knockout mouse report establishes the core mismatch: the mouse neocortex is essentially normal despite DCX loss, whereas the human neocortical phenotype (lissencephaly/SBH) is severe.

evidence.snippet: Paradoxically, genetic deletion of Dcx in mice does not cause neocortical malformation.
evidence.explanation: Documents the acute-knockdown-versus-germline-knockout discrepancy: acute in utero RNAi of DCX reproduces the migration defect that germline deletion does not, one of the Romero review's flagged model caveats.

evidence.snippet: In utero RNAi in the rat consistently leads to both the formation of SBH and laminar displacement of transfected cells in normotopic cortex, whereas the same treatment in mouse fails to induce SBH but does create laminar displacement.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates a genuine rat-versus-mouse species difference in the Dcx-loss neocortical phenotype, so even acute knockdown does not model the severe human heterotopia in mouse.

evidence.snippet: Humans with mutations show profound alterations in cortical lamination, whereas in mouse, RNAi-mediated knockdown but not germline knockout shows abnormal positioning of cortical neurons.
evidence.explanation: Identifies partially redundant Dclk compensation as a mechanistic explanation for why the germline Dcx-knockout mouse under-reproduces the human phenotype, supporting the redundancy arm of the mismatch.

open_questions/1.rationale: DCX is one of the most striking human/model discordances in the cortical malformation literature, and it bears directly on how strongly the mouse can validate the DCX branch of this entry. In humans, X-linked DCX mutations cause classic thick lissencephaly in males and subcortical band heterotopia in females — a severe, defining neocortical migration defect. Yet the germline Dcx-knockout mouse has neocortical lamination largely indistinguishable from wild type, with the migration/lamination phenotype restricted to the hippocampus; the neocortical malformation only appears when Dcx is acutely silenced by in utero RNAi rather than deleted in the germline. Two overlapping explanations are documented: (1) developmental compensation / genetic redundancy, whereby the paralog doublecortin-like kinase (Dclk) substitutes for Dcx in the germline knockout but not under acute knockdown, so that only Dcx/Dclk compound loss reproduces the migration defect; and (2) a genuine species difference, since the same in utero RNAi against Dcx induces band heterotopia in rat but fails to induce heterotopia in mouse. This is a concrete instance of two knowledge gaps flagged by the Romero, Bahi-Buisson & Francis 2018 cortical-malformation review that seeds this epic: that mouse models often fail to reproduce human MCD features, and that acute in utero knockdown can be more severe than germline knockout because of off-target effects, developmental compensation, or redundancy revealed only by double knockouts. Mechanistically it leaves open whether the human neocortical lesion reflects reduced Dcx/Dclk-family redundancy in human migrating neurons, a rat-like rather than mouse-like species requirement for Dcx in neocortical radial migration, or a human-specific progenitor/outer-radial-glia context — meaning the mouse germline knockout, taken alone, validates the DCX microtubule-stabilization mechanism only weakly for the human neocortical phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in PIEZO1, which encodes a mechanically activated ion channel, have been reported with autosomal dominant dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis and non-immune hydrops of unknown aetiology.
evidence.explanation: Identifies PIEZO1 as a mechanically activated ion channel and the causal gene locus for this disorder.

evidence.snippet: No truncated PIEZO1 protein products were identified in western blot analysis in GLD1:II.3 and GLD2:II.2
evidence.explanation: Direct protein-level demonstration that truncating alleles yield no stable PIEZO1 protein, i.e. loss of function.

evidence.snippet: Patch-clamp analysis of the missense PIEZO1 channel in a heterologous system (a mammalian cell line derived from HEK293T cells) indicated strongly diminished current amplitudes as compared with wild type, likely due to reduced cell surface expression.
evidence.explanation: Electrophysiological confirmation that the patient missense allele is hypomorphic/loss-of-function.

evidence.snippet: PIEZO1 variants have been associated with generalized lymphatic dysplasia (GLD) through mechanisms involving reduced PIEZO1 expression. Here, we report variants where the mechanism involves reduced channel mechanical sensitivity.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the second loss-of-function route: mechanical insensitivity of an expressed channel, distinct from reduced expression.

steps/1.description: Biallelic nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, and missense variants in PIEZO1 abolish or severely reduce the activity of a mechanically activated, calcium-permeable cation channel. Two mechanistically distinct routes to loss of function are documented: reduced or absent PIEZO1 protein (truncating and splice variants, shown by western blot to eliminate or reduce PIEZO1 expression) and reduced channel mechanical sensitivity despite surface expression (cap and sub-cap missense variants that are mechanically insensitive yet partly rescuable with the chemical agonist Yoda1).

evidence.snippet: Piezo1 knockdown in cultured lymphatic endothelial cells inhibited the laminar flow-induced calcium influx
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that PIEZO1 is required for flow-induced calcium signalling in lymphatic endothelial cells.

evidence.snippet: Yoda1 rapidly triggered nuclear FOXO1 extrusion in WT mesenteries but not in Piezo1LEC–/– mesenteries, confirming the PIEZO1/FOXO1 axis in mesenteric lymphatics
evidence.explanation: Ex vivo mouse mesenteric lymphatics lacking endothelial PIEZO1 fail to transduce channel activation into a downstream signalling response, demonstrating that PIEZO1 loss abolishes lymphatic endothelial mechanosignalling.

steps/2.description: PIEZO1 is abundantly expressed in lymphatic endothelial cells, where it transduces oscillatory shear stress and membrane stretch into calcium entry. Loss of PIEZO1 abrogates flow-induced calcium influx and the downstream ORAI1/KLF2/Notch transcriptional programme that drives lymphatic sprouting, and it removes the mechanical cue required for valve-forming cell behaviour.

evidence.snippet: activation of the mechanosensory channel PIEZO1 in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) caused rapid exocytosis of the TIE ligand ANGPT2, ectodomain shedding of TIE1 by disintegrin and metalloproteinase domain-containing protein 17 (ADAM17), and increased TIE/PI3K/AKT signaling, followed by nuclear export of the transcription factor FOXO1
evidence.explanation: Establishes the PIEZO1 to ANGPT2/TIE/PI3K-AKT/FOXO1 signaling axis in lymphatic endothelial cells.

steps/3.description: PIEZO1 activation in lymphatic endothelial cells triggers rapid exocytosis of the TIE ligand ANGPT2, ADAM17-mediated ectodomain shedding of TIE1, increased TIE/PI3K/AKT signaling, and nuclear export of the transcription factor FOXO1. Loss of PIEZO1 function therefore silences a signaling network whose other members (ANGPT2, TIE1) are themselves mutated in primary lymphedema, providing a molecular bridge between channel function and lymphatic gene expression.

evidence.snippet: we analyzed two mouse lines lacking PIEZO1 in endothelial cells (via Tie2Cre or Lyve1Cre) and found that they exhibited pleural effusion and died postnatally. Strikingly, the number of lymphatic valves was dramatically reduced in these mice.
evidence.explanation: Endothelial Piezo1 loss reduces lymphatic valve number and reproduces pleural effusion in mice.

evidence.snippet: the process of protrusion in the valve leaflets, which is associated with collective cell migration, actin polymerization, and remodeling of cell-cell junctions, was impaired in Tie2Cre;Piezo1cKO mice
evidence.explanation: Identifies the specific cellular step of valve morphogenesis that requires PIEZO1.

evidence.snippet: Lymphatic-specific conditional Piezo1 knockout largely phenocopied sprouting defects shown in Orai1- or Klf2- knockout lymphatics during embryo development. Postnatal deletion of Piezo1 induced lymphatic regression in adults.
evidence.explanation: Shows PIEZO1 is required both for developmental lymphatic sprouting and for maintenance of adult lymphatics.

evidence.snippet: PIEZO1 is required for lymphatic valve formation, and several lymphatic abnormalities have been reported to be associated with autosomal recessive PIEZO1 pathogenic variants including neonatal hydrops, lymphedema involving various body regions, and chylothorax.
evidence.explanation: Connects the valve-formation requirement to the human autosomal recessive PIEZO1 clinical spectrum.

steps/4.description: Endothelial-specific Piezo1 deletion in mice dramatically reduces the number of lymphatic valves and impairs the collective cell migration, actin polymerization, and cell-cell junction remodeling that produce the valve leaflet, while lymphatic-specific deletion phenocopies the sprouting defects of Orai1 and Klf2 knockouts and postnatal deletion causes lymphatic regression. Lymphatic valves are essential for unidirectional lymph flow, so their loss renders the collecting lymphatics incompetent.

evidence.snippet: Generalized lymphatic dysplasia (GLD) is a rare form of primary lymphoedema characterized by a uniform, widespread lymphoedema affecting all segments of the body, with systemic involvement such as intestinal and/or pulmonary lymphangiectasia, pleural effusions, chylothoraces and/or pericardial effusions.
evidence.explanation: Defines the generalized, multi-compartment lymphatic dysplasia phenotype that PIEZO1 loss produces.

evidence.snippet: The rerouting suggests failure of superficial lymphatic collector function.
evidence.explanation: Lymphoscintigraphic evidence that the functional lesion is collector failure, consistent with the valve defect.

steps/5.description: The resulting disorder is a uniform, widespread lymphatic dysplasia affecting all body segments, with systemic involvement of the thoracic, pericardial, and intestinal lymphatics. Lymphoscintigraphy in affected individuals shows a strikingly consistent and symmetric pattern of deep and superficial rerouting, indicating failure of superficial lymphatic collector function rather than simple aplasia.

evidence.snippet: One cause of NIHF is lymphatic malformation 6 (LMPHM6) due to biallelic loss-of-function (LoF) variants in PIEZO1.
evidence.explanation: Directly attributes non-immune hydrops fetalis to biallelic loss-of-function PIEZO1 (LMPHM6).

evidence.snippet: biallelic variants have a high incidence of NIHF (7 of the 10 affected cases). This may be lethal in the perinatal period (n=2).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the frequency and perinatal lethality of hydrops in the founding cohort.

steps/6.description: In utero, lymphatic transport failure produces non-immune hydrops fetalis with pleural and pericardial effusions and ascites. This may be lethal in the perinatal period; in survivors the neonatal edema often resolves completely, but chylothorax may persist or recur.

evidence.snippet: Survivors may present later with lymphoedema of the peripheries (mainly lower limbs but also arms (n=4), face (n=3) and genitalia (n=1)), with or without chylothoraces (n=2) and intestinal lymphangiectasia (n=1).
evidence.explanation: Documents the postnatal distribution of lymphedema and its systemic complications.

steps/7.description: Survivors typically re-present in childhood with lymphedema of the lower limbs, arms, face, and genitalia, with or without chylothoraces and intestinal lymphangiectasia. Recurrent severe facial cellulitis complicates the facial lymphedema and is a major source of morbidity.

edges/1.description: Loss of PIEZO1 channel function removes the principal mechanosensor by which lymphatic endothelial cells convert flow and stretch into calcium influx.

edges/2.description: PIEZO1 activation is the upstream trigger for ANGPT2 exocytosis and TIE pathway engagement in lymphatic endothelial cells.

edges/3.description: Loss of flow-triggered mechanotransduction removes the signal driving valve-leaflet protrusion and flow-activated lymphatic sprouting.

edges/4.description: Loss of this transcriptional output contributes to defective lymphatic vessel and valve development.

edges/5.description: Incompetent, hypoplastic lymphatic collectors cannot clear interstitial fluid and chyle.

edges/6.description: Failure of thoracic and abdominal lymph drainage causes chyle and serous fluid to accumulate in body cavities, presenting in utero as hydrops.

edges/7.description: Failure of superficial collector function causes interstitial protein-rich fluid to accumulate in the limbs, face, and genitalia.

evidence.snippet: Here we report homozygous and compound heterozygous mutations in PIEZO1, resulting in an autosomal recessive form of GLD with a high incidence of non-immune hydrops fetalis and childhood onset of facial and four limb lymphoedema.
evidence.explanation: Establishes PIEZO1 as the causal gene, with biallelic variants, for this form of generalized lymphatic dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: Our results delineate a novel clinical category of PIEZO1-associated hereditary lymphoedema.
evidence.explanation: Independent contemporaneous report establishing PIEZO1-associated hereditary lymphedema as a distinct entity.

evidence.snippet: PIEZO1 variants causing AR NIHF were characterized by loss of function and isolated NIHF phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that the recessive (LMPHM6) mechanism is loss of function, in contrast to the dominant gain-of-function red-cell disease.

evidence.snippet: She subsequently had recurrent pleural effusions involving both pleural cavities, which tended to improve with restriction of her fat intake, and, one occasion, subcutaneous octreotide.
evidence.explanation: Documents clinical improvement of the recurrent effusions with dietary fat restriction in a molecularly confirmed LMPHM6 patient.

treatments/0.description: Restriction of long-chain dietary fat, with medium-chain triglyceride substitution, reduces chyle production and thoracic-duct lymph flow and is first-line conservative management of chylothorax and enteric lymph loss in LMPHM6.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Reducing long-chain fat intake lowers chyle flow into the incompetent thoracic lymphatics, reducing effusion volume.

evidence.snippet: She subsequently had recurrent pleural effusions involving both pleural cavities, which tended to improve with restriction of her fat intake, and, one occasion, subcutaneous octreotide.
evidence.explanation: Single-patient use of subcutaneous octreotide alongside dietary fat restriction; the report does not isolate the octreotide effect, so support is partial.

treatments/1.description: Subcutaneous octreotide, a somatostatin analogue that reduces splanchnic blood flow and lymph production, has been used as adjunctive therapy for refractory chylothorax in LMPHM6. Evidence is limited to single-patient experience.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Somatostatin-analogue reduction of lymph production decreases chyle accumulation in the pleural space.

evidence.snippet: Four patients of our cohort had severe, recurrent facial cellulitis with significant morbidity (high pyrexia and frequent admission to intensive care).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the clinical burden (recurrent severe cellulitis complicating lymphedema) that skin care and prompt antibiotic treatment address; the paper does not itself report a supportive-care trial, so support is partial.

treatments/2.description: Complete decongestive therapy - compression garments or bandaging, manual lymphatic drainage, exercise, and meticulous skin care - is the mainstay of chronic lymphedema management, together with prompt antibiotic treatment of cellulitis, which is a major source of morbidity in this disorder.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Decongestive therapy mechanically compensates for failed lymphatic collector function.

evidence.snippet: we detected one rare and previously unobserved homozygous missense variant in PIEZO1 (c.5162C>G, p.Ser1721Trp) as a novel genetic cause of autosomal recessive LMPHM6, in a family with three adverse pregnancy outcomes due to nonimmune fetal hydrops
evidence.explanation: Recurrent pregnancy loss in a single family illustrates the recurrence risk that counseling and molecular diagnosis address.

treatments/3.description: Counseling covers autosomal recessive inheritance and the 25% sibling recurrence risk, carrier testing, and prenatal or preimplantation genetic testing options once the familial biallelic PIEZO1 genotype is known. Recurrent adverse pregnancy outcomes are a recognized presentation.

evidence.snippet: Patch-clamp studies of the cap and sub-cap variant channels revealed abolished or reduced channel mechanical sensitivity with the possibility to activate the channels and partly rescue mechanical sensitivity by the small molecule Yoda1.
evidence.explanation: In vitro pharmacological rescue of variant channels; no clinical evidence exists, so support for this as a treatment is partial.

evidence.snippet: we assessed a potential therapeutic value of Piezo1 activation in lymphatic regeneration and found that a Piezo1 agonist, Yoda1, effectively suppressed postsurgical lymphedema development.
evidence.explanation: Mouse proof of concept that PIEZO1 agonism can reduce lymphedema; the model is acquired postsurgical lymphedema, not biallelic PIEZO1 disease.

treatments/4.description: The small-molecule PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 partly rescues the mechanical sensitivity of mechanically insensitive LMPHM6 missense channels in vitro, and an analogue with improved potency has been synthesized. This is a preclinical, genotype-restricted concept - it cannot rescue null alleles, and systemic PIEZO1 activation would also act on erythrocytes and the blood vasculature. No PIEZO1-directed therapy is approved.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Chemical agonism partly restores mechanical activation of variant channels that are expressed but mechanically insensitive.

evidence.snippet: Treatment has proved very difficult and has involved pleurodesis, ligation of the thoracic duct and pleuro-peritoneal shunting.
evidence.explanation: Documents the interventional options actually used in a molecularly confirmed LMPHM6 patient, while explicitly recording that control was difficult - so this supports use, not efficacy.

evidence.snippet: Despite pleurodesis, his effusions are persistent resulting in a restrictive lung defect and nocturnal hypoventilation requiring non-invasive ventilation (NIV).
evidence.explanation: A second affected individual in whom pleurodesis failed to control chylous effusion, recording the limits of the intervention.

treatments/5.description: Pleurodesis, thoracic-duct ligation, and pleuro-peritoneal shunting are the standard escalation options when chylous pleural effusion recurs despite dietary fat restriction and octreotide. In LMPHM6 they are documented as used, not as effective: in the one reported adolescent-onset family, effusion control proved very difficult despite all three, and the proband's father had persistent effusions and a restrictive lung defect after pleurodesis. No LMPHM6-specific response rate has been established for any of these procedures, and none targets the underlying lymphatic mechanism.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: Obliterating the pleural space or diverting/interrupting thoracic-duct flow limits accumulation of chyle in the pleural cavity; the incompetent lymphatic network itself is unaltered.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with a role in the repair of ICLs by homologous recombination (HR), knockdown of MCM8 or MCM9 significantly reduces HR repair efficiency.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports reduced homologous-recombination repair after MCM8 loss.

evidence.snippet: Chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis using human DR-GFP cells or Xenopus egg extract demonstrated that MCM8 and MCM9 proteins are rapidly recruited to DNA damage sites and promote RAD51 recruitment.
evidence.explanation: This places MCM8 upstream of RAD51 loading during homologous recombination.

evidence.snippet: chromatin recruitment of HR factors like Rad51 and RPA is impaired and HR strongly reduced.
evidence.explanation: Mcm8-deficient cells fail to load RAD51, confirming the homologous-recombination defect in vivo.

steps/1.description: Biallelic MCM8 loss disables the MCM8-MCM9 helicase, reducing RAD51 recruitment and homologous-recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks. This genome-maintenance defect is especially damaging during meiosis, where programmed double-strand breaks must be repaired by homologous recombination.

evidence.snippet: MCM8(-/-) mice are sterile because spermatocytes are blocked in meiotic prophase I, and females have only arrested primary follicles and frequently develop ovarian tumors.
evidence.explanation: This documents prophase I arrest with germ-cell depletion in both sexes on MCM8 loss.

steps/2.description: Germ cells that cannot complete homologous recombination arrest during meiotic prophase I and are eliminated rather than maturing into functional gametes, depleting the germ-cell pool in both sexes.

evidence.snippet: Here, we studied 3 sisters with primary amenorrhea, hypothyroidism, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
evidence.explanation: This documents ovarian failure with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism as the founding female phenotype of biallelic MCM8 deficiency.

steps/3.description: Loss of oocytes during meiotic progression depletes the ovarian reserve, presenting clinically as primary ovarian insufficiency, ovarian dysgenesis, primary amenorrhea, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism in 46,XX individuals.

evidence.snippet: two consanguineous families presenting as primary amenorrhoea in the females and as small testes and azoospermia in a male.
evidence.explanation: This directly documents the male spermatogenic-failure branch as small testes with azoospermia.

evidence.snippet: The testes tissue sections in the male showed a Sertoli cell-only syndrome (SCOS).
evidence.explanation: This adds Sertoli cell-only histology as the testicular correlate of the male MCM8 phenotype.

steps/4.description: In 46,XY individuals, MCM8-dependent meiotic failure in spermatocytes produces spermatogenic arrest with small testes, non-obstructive azoospermia, and Sertoli cell-only histology.

evidence.snippet: both biallelic MCM8 and MCM9 variants are linked to hypogonadism and the early development of germ cell tumors.
evidence.explanation: This establishes early-onset germ cell tumors as the human cancer branch of biallelic MCM8 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: MCM8(-/-) mice are sterile because spermatocytes are blocked in meiotic prophase I, and females have only arrested primary follicles and frequently develop ovarian tumors.
evidence.explanation: The ovarian tumors of Mcm8-null mice provide model-organism support for a gonadal tumor-predisposition branch.

steps/5.description: Beyond the gonads, MCM8-dependent homologous-recombination failure produces a somatic genome-instability state. In humans this is associated with an emerging predisposition to early-onset germ cell tumors; murine Mcm8 loss likewise produces ovarian tumors. This cancer profile is narrower than the gastrointestinal polyposis / colorectal-cancer spectrum reported for MCM9.

evidence.snippet: Here, we studied 3 sisters with primary amenorrhea, hypothyroidism, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
evidence.explanation: The founding family establishes the ovarian-failure phenotype tied to a biallelic MCM8 variant.

steps/6.description: Reported 46,XX individuals present with primary ovarian insufficiency or ovarian dysgenesis, often with primary amenorrhea and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

steps/7.description: In 46,XY individuals the disorder manifests as severe non-obstructive azoospermia, frequently with small testes.

evidence.snippet: both biallelic MCM8 and MCM9 variants are linked to hypogonadism and the early development of germ cell tumors.
evidence.explanation: This supports early-onset germ cell tumors as the cancer phenotype linked to biallelic MCM8 variants.

steps/8.description: Biallelic MCM8 variant carriers show an association with early-onset germ cell tumors, a narrower cancer spectrum than the gastrointestinal malignancy reported for MCM9.

evidence.snippet: deficiency for these genes impairs homologous recombination (HR)-mediated DNA repair during gametogenesis and somatic cells cycles.
evidence.explanation: This links the recombination defect to failed gametogenesis in Mcm8-deficient animals.

edges/1.description: Germline cells are highly sensitive to MCM8-dependent genome-maintenance failure: unresolved meiotic recombination intermediates block progression through prophase I.

edges/2.description: In 46,XX individuals, germ-cell depletion exhausts the ovarian follicle pool and produces primary ovarian insufficiency.

edges/3.description: In 46,XY individuals, the same germ-cell depletion produces spermatogenic failure presenting as non-obstructive azoospermia.

edges/4.description: The female branch presents clinically as primary / premature ovarian insufficiency.

edges/5.description: In 46,XY individuals severe spermatogenic failure manifests clinically as non-obstructive azoospermia.

edges/6.description: The somatic instability state drives an early-onset neoplasia phenotype, especially gonadal germ cell tumors.

evidence.snippet: SNP analysis and whole-exome sequencing revealed the presence of a pathogenic variant of the minichromosome maintenance 8 gene (MCM8, c.446C>G; p.P149R) located within a region of homozygosity
evidence.explanation: This establishes MCM8 as the causal gene in the founding female family.

evidence.snippet: A homozygous frameshift mutation c.998delG (p. Gly333Glufs*50) in MCM8 was identified in the two siblings.
evidence.explanation: This extends the causal role of biallelic MCM8 loss-of-function variants to a bisexual gonadal-failure family.

genes/0.notes: MCM8 encodes minichromosome maintenance 8 homologous recombination repair factor, which partners with MCM9 as a helicase that promotes RAD51-dependent homologous recombination.

evidence.snippet: Here, we studied 3 sisters with primary amenorrhea, hypothyroidism, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
evidence.explanation: This anchors the ovarian-failure branch to the hypergonadotropic hypogonadism that drives hormone-replacement treatment.

evidence.snippet: This review outlines key diagnostic criteria, initial investigations, referral pathways and management options including hormone therapy, chronic disease risk reduction, fertility counselling and psychosocial support.
evidence.explanation: This provides condition-level management evidence that hormone therapy is part of standard care for primary ovarian insufficiency, the core female branch of MCM8-related disease.

treatments/0.description: Estrogen-based hormone replacement is used to treat hypoestrogenism in the ovarian-failure branch, support pubertal development, and reduce osteoporosis risk.

evidence.snippet: These findings underscore the importance of including MCM8/MCM9 in diagnostic gene panels for certain clinical contexts and suggest that biallelic carriers may benefit from cancer surveillance.
evidence.explanation: This supports cancer surveillance for biallelic MCM8 carriers given the germ cell tumor risk.

treatments/1.description: Because biallelic MCM8 deficiency is associated with early-onset germ cell tumors, affected individuals may benefit from cancer surveillance, including imaging for gonadal or extragonadal germ cell tumors.

evidence.snippet: expands the mutational spectrum of MCM8 involved in male NOA and female POI and provides a new molecular marker for genetic counseling of infertility.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports genetic counseling as part of management for MCM8-associated gonadal failure.

treatments/2.description: Genetic counseling is appropriate for affected families because the condition is recessive, causes infertility in both sexes, and carries implications for reproductive planning and cancer surveillance.

evidence.snippet: confirmed that affected family members were heterozygous for the presence of an intragenic duplication encompassing exons 3 to 5 of RUNX2
evidence.explanation: Identifies the causal structural variant in the founding pedigree.

evidence.snippet: These three exons code for the Q/A domain and the functionally essential DNA-binding runt domain of RUNX2.
evidence.explanation: Establishes which functional domains the duplicated interval encodes.

evidence.snippet: The results demonstrated that the intronic breakpoints of the duplication differed from those previously found in the French Canadian family, but that the consequences on RUNX2 transcript were identical.
evidence.explanation: Supports the claim that the transcript consequence, not the breakpoint, is the shared lesion.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous tandem duplication inside RUNX2, spanning exons 3 to 5, 3 to 6, or 3 to 7 in the reported families. The duplicated interval encodes the Q/A domain and the DNA-binding runt domain, so the mutant transcript carries a second copy of the functionally essential part of the protein. Breakpoints differ between families while the consequence on the transcript is the same, which argues that the duplicated exon content rather than any particular breakpoint is what matters.

evidence.snippet: Until now, only loss-of-function mutations have been detected in RUNX2; the present report associates an apparent gain-of-function alteration of RUNX2 function with a distinct rare disease.
evidence.explanation: States explicitly that this is a gain-of-function RUNX2 disease, in contrast with every previously known RUNX2 allele.

steps/2.description: RUNX2 is the master transcription factor of osteoblast differentiation and of the chondrocyte hypertrophy that precedes endochondral bone formation. In MDMHB it is present at raised cellular levels and acts as a gain of function. This is the mirror image of cleidocranial dysplasia, where RUNX2 haploinsufficiency causes clavicular hypoplasia and delayed cranial ossification, and it is why the skeletal phenotypes of the two RUNX2 diseases barely overlap: the clavicles are enlarged here and hypoplastic or absent there.

evidence.snippet: We review previously reported cases with MDMHB and highlight the resemblance of this disorder with Pyle disease, which may be explained by intersecting molecular pathways between RUNX2 and sFRP4.
evidence.explanation: Source for the Pyle-disease resemblance and the proposed pathway intersection described in this node.

steps/3.description: Failure of the normal funnelling of the metaphysis produces flaring of the long-bone metaphyses with thin cortices and an osteoporotic radiographic appearance, together with enlargement of the medial halves of the clavicles. Metaphyseal funnelling is osteoclastic resorption of the periosteal surface as the bone lengthens, which is why the node is bound to bone resorption and the osteoclast alongside the chondrocyte-side endochondral terms - the same resorption step whose failure produces the Erlenmeyer-flask metaphysis of Pyle disease. This radiographic combination is close enough to Pyle disease to have been proposed as evidence that RUNX2 and sFRP4 act on intersecting pathways in metaphyseal modelling.

evidence.snippet: Facial manifestations include beaked nose, short philtrum, thin lips, maxillary hypoplasia, dystrophic yellowish teeth.
evidence.explanation: The original clinical description of the craniofacial and dental phenotype.

steps/4.description: Maxillary hypoplasia with a beaked nose, short philtrum and thin lips, plus dystrophic yellowish teeth. The dental component is often what brings affected people to medical attention, ahead of any skeletal complaint.

evidence.snippet: Metaphyseal dysplasia with maxillary hypoplasia and brachydactyly (MDMHB) is an autosomal-dominant bone dysplasia characterized by metaphyseal flaring of long bones, enlargement of the medial halves of the clavicles, maxillary hypoplasia, variable brachydactyly, and dystrophic teeth.
evidence.explanation: Defines the expressed skeletal phenotype recorded in this node.

steps/5.description: The expressed skeletal disease: flared metaphyses, enlarged medial clavicles, thin cortices, mild osteoporosis, genu valgum, and disproportionate short stature with variable brachydactyly.

evidence.snippet: highlight the importance of considering an underlying skeletal dysplasia in patients presenting with significant dental problems and other suggestive features, including disproportionate short stature and/or digital anomalies
evidence.explanation: States the diagnostic implication that defines this node.

steps/6.description: Significant dental problems, usually in childhood or adolescence, are the route by which most affected people enter the diagnostic pathway. Recognising the skeletal dysplasia behind them is the clinical lesson of the disorder.

evidence.snippet: Transfection studies with murine Runx2 cDNA showed that cellular levels of mutated RUNX2 were markedly higher than those of wild-type RUNX2, suggesting that the RUNX2 duplication found in individuals with MDMHB leads to a gain of function.
evidence.explanation: The functional experiment that establishes this edge.

edges/1.description: The duplication-bearing transcript yields markedly higher cellular protein levels than wild-type RUNX2 in transfection assays.

evidence.snippet: Clinical and radiographic examination revealed mild facial dysmorphism, dental anomalies, enlarged clavicles, genua valga and metaphyseal flaring and thin cortices with an osteoporotic skeletal appearance.
evidence.explanation: Documents the metaphyseal flaring with thin cortices that this node produces.

edges/2.description: Raised RUNX2 activity in the growth plate and metaphyseal osteoblast compartment disturbs the modelling that normally narrows the metaphysis as the bone lengthens.

evidence.snippet: Runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2) is well-known for its role in bone development and tooth morphogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes RUNX2's role in tooth morphogenesis, the basis for linking the dental phenotype to the same transcription factor. Note the cohort in that paper carries a whole-gene rather than an intragenic RUNX2 duplication, so it is cited here for the gene's role, not as an MDMHB case series.

edges/3.description: The same transcription factor governs maxillary intramembranous ossification and tooth morphogenesis, which is why the craniofacial and dental features travel with the metaphyseal ones.

evidence.snippet: Metaphyseal dysplasia with maxillary hypoplasia and brachydactyly (MDMHB) is an autosomal-dominant skeletal dysplasia characterised by metaphyseal flaring of the long bones, enlargement of the medial halves of the clavicles, maxillary hypoplasia, brachydactyly, dental anomalies and mild osteoporosis.
evidence.explanation: Lists mild osteoporosis alongside the metaphyseal flaring, which is the link this edge asserts.

edges/4.description: Flared metaphyses with thin cortices translate clinically into an osteoporotic skeleton and genu valgum.

evidence.snippet: Dental problems were the primary presenting feature in all four affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Direct evidence that the dental phenotype leads the presentation.

edges/5.description: The dental anomalies are severe enough to dominate presentation.

evidence.snippet: Metaphyseal dysplasia with maxillary hypoplasia with or without brachydactyly (MDMHB) is an ultra-rare skeletal dysplasia caused by heterozygous intragenic RUNX2 duplications, comprising either exons 3 to 5 or exons 3 to 6 of RUNX2.
evidence.explanation: States the causal variant class and the duplicated exon intervals.

evidence.snippet: Analysis for copy-number variations revealed that a 105 kb duplication within RUNX2 segregated with the MDMHB phenotype in a region with maximum linkage.
evidence.explanation: Segregation evidence establishing RUNX2 as the causal locus.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous intragenic tandem duplication spanning RUNX2 exons 3-5, 3-6 or 3-7. Because this is a copy-number change inside a gene, exome or targeted sequencing must be analysed for intragenic CNVs; plain variant calling will miss it. The same gene causes cleidocranial dysplasia by loss of function, so the direction of the RUNX2 lesion, not merely its presence, determines which disease results.

evidence.snippet: Dental problems were the primary presenting feature in all four affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the dental burden that this management addresses. No disease-modifying therapy exists.

treatments/0.description: Management is symptomatic and led by dentistry, since the dental anomalies are the dominant clinical burden and the usual presenting problem.

evidence.snippet: Metaphyseal dysplasia with maxillary hypoplasia and brachydactyly (MDMHB) is an autosomal-dominant bone dysplasia characterized by metaphyseal flaring of long bones, enlargement of the medial halves of the clavicles, maxillary hypoplasia, variable brachydactyly, and dystrophic teeth.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the dominant inheritance on which the recurrence risk rests.

treatments/1.description: Dominant inheritance with a 50% recurrence risk for offspring, though de novo cases occur. Counselling depends on recognising that the RUNX2 lesion here is a duplication rather than a loss-of-function variant.

evidence.snippet: Transfection studies with murine Runx2 cDNA showed that cellular levels of mutated RUNX2 were markedly higher than those of wild-type RUNX2, suggesting that the RUNX2 duplication found in individuals with MDMHB leads to a gain of function.
evidence.explanation: The observation the gap is built on, and the hedged wording that leaves the mechanism open.

evidence.snippet: We describe here the oro-dental phenotype of four patients of a unique family with a 285 kb duplication including the entire sequence of RUNX2, likely responsible for three functional copies of the gene, leading to an increased RUNX2 dosage.
evidence.explanation: The whole-gene duplication comparator referred to in the rationale; it raises RUNX2 dosage without the intragenic rearrangement, so its phenotype bears on which model is right.

open_questions/0.rationale: The transfection experiment shows raised levels of the duplication-bearing protein and the authors themselves phrase the conclusion as an apparent gain of function. Two quite different models fit that observation: a stabilised or degradation-resistant protein present at higher steady-state level, or a structurally altered factor with a duplicated runt domain and changed DNA-binding or partner behaviour. The distinction matters because only the first predicts that a whole-gene RUNX2 duplication should produce the same skeletal disease, and the reported whole-gene duplication family has a predominantly oro-dental phenotype rather than the full MDMHB picture. No study has separated the two models.

evidence.snippet: We identified six homozygous exonic mutations in the seven unrelated patients with PAM we studied.
evidence.explanation: One of the two 2006 papers establishing SLC34A2 as the causal gene, quoted at its primary genetic finding.

evidence.snippet: Although the protein from the Thr468del construct was synthesised and expressed in the oocyte membrane, phosphate transport was similar to non-injected control oocytes.
evidence.explanation: Evidence for the second allelic route: a variant protein that is made and detected in the membrane while transporting no more phosphate than an uninjected control.

evidence.snippet: the Thr468del mutant does not function properly or may not be sufficiently expressed in the membrane, or a combination of both
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL, and included specifically to carry the authors' own hedge rather than the cleaner claim their data are often used for. They decline to separate impaired function from insufficient membrane expression, so this node states the disjunction they state rather than resolving it for them.

steps/1.description: Homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SLC34A2, identified independently by two groups in 2006 in unrelated families. Some variants abolish the protein outright. Others reduce transport without abolishing production: in oocyte expression studies the Thr468del protein was synthesised and detected in the membrane while moving no more phosphate than uninjected controls. The authors of that work decline to claim a clean membrane-resident-but-transport-dead mechanism, concluding instead that the mutant either does not function properly or is not sufficiently expressed in the membrane, or both, and that hedge is preserved here. Either way the practical consequence holds: detecting the transporter protein does not establish that it works.

evidence.snippet: Normally, phosphate will be cleared from the alveolar space by transport via NaPi-2b located in the apical membrane of the alveolar type II cell.
evidence.explanation: States the normal physiology this node breaks, including the cell type and the membrane face on which the transporter sits.

evidence.snippet: Na+ shapes the Pi-binding pocket and drives the transition from the outward-open to occluded state
evidence.explanation: Structural basis for sodium-driven transport, which is why a variant can abolish transport activity while leaving the protein in place.

steps/2.description: NaPi-IIb normally sits on the apical, air-facing membrane of the alveolar type II cell and uses the sodium gradient to haul phosphate out of the lining fluid and back into the cell. Structural work has since shown the transporter works by an elevator mechanism, in which the phosphate-binding site rides through the membrane and sodium binding drives the transition between states, which explains how a variant can disable transport without removing the protein.

evidence.snippet: this leads to an excess of phosphate in the alveolar lumen with subsequent precipitation of extracellular calcium
evidence.explanation: States the accumulation and the resulting calcium precipitation, which is exactly the transition this node models.

steps/3.description: Phosphate released by the continual catabolism of surfactant phospholipid accumulates in the alveolar lining fluid until the fluid supersaturates with respect to calcium phosphate, at which point calcium precipitates with it. This is the step at which a transport defect becomes a mineral one.

evidence.snippet: Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis (PAM) is a rare hereditary disease of abnormal phosphate transport associated with accumulation of calcium phosphate crystals within the alveolar airspaces of the lung.
evidence.explanation: Names the composition and the location of the deposits in one sentence, and attributes them to abnormal phosphate transport.

steps/4.description: Concentrically laminated calcium phosphate concretions accumulate within the alveolar air spaces. They are the defining lesion, the source of the characteristic sandstorm radiograph, and, importantly, the driver of what follows rather than an end product of it.

evidence.snippet: epithelial deletion of Npt2b in mice results in a progressive pulmonary process characterized by diffuse alveolar microlith accumulation
evidence.explanation: Establishes the mouse model and its progressive microlith phenotype. The phospholipidosis is reported in the same sentence in the source as an unexpected component of that phenotype.

steps/5.description: Accumulation of surfactant phospholipid in the alveolar space, found unexpectedly in the epithelial Npt2b-deletion mouse. It is worth carrying because it is mechanistically odd: the same lipid whose breakdown supplies the phosphate that forms the stones also accumulates, which suggests the transporter defect perturbs surfactant handling more broadly than the simple phosphate-bailing account predicts.

evidence.snippet: Microliths introduced by adoptive transfer into the lungs of wild-type mice produce marked macrophage-rich inflammation and elevation of serum MCP-1 that peaks at 1 week and resolves at 1 month, concomitant with clearance of stones.
evidence.explanation: The adoptive-transfer and resolution result, which establishes the direction of causation between stones and inflammation rather than merely their co-occurrence.

steps/6.description: Macrophage-rich inflammation provoked by the stones themselves.
